questions.stem: According to the Bronsted-Lowry theory, a base is a substance that
questions.explanation: The Bronsted-Lowry model defines acids and bases by proton transfer, so a base is a proton acceptor. Ammonia is a good example: it accepts an H+ from water to form NH4+ even though it contains no hydroxide ion of its own.

distractorRationale.a: A proton donor is the Bronsted-Lowry definition of an acid
distractorRationale.c: Accepting an electron pair is the Lewis definition of an acid, not a Bronsted-Lowry base
distractorRationale.d: Producing hydrogen ions is the Arrhenius definition of an acid

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a strong acid from a concentrated acid?

options.text: A strong acid contains more acid per unit volume than a concentrated one
A strong acid ionises almost completely in water, while a concentrated acid simply has a large amount of solute per unit volume
A strong acid always has a lower pH than any concentrated acid
There is no difference; the terms mean the same thing

questions.explanation: Strength is about the extent of ionisation, which is a fixed property of the acid itself. Concentration is about how much acid is dissolved and can be changed simply by adding water. A dilute solution of hydrochloric acid is strong but not concentrated, while glacial ethanoic acid is concentrated but weak.

distractorRationale.a: Amount per unit volume is the definition of concentration, not strength
distractorRationale.c: A very dilute strong acid can have a higher pH than a concentrated weak acid
distractorRationale.d: The two terms describe entirely different properties and are not interchangeable

questions.stem: A colourless gas that turns lime water milky is produced when a dilute acid is added to
questions.explanation: Acids react with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide: CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. Carbon dioxide is the gas that turns lime water milky by forming insoluble calcium carbonate.

distractorRationale.a: Zinc gives hydrogen, which burns with a pop and has no effect on lime water
distractorRationale.b: Neutralisation with an alkali produces only salt and water, with no gas at all
distractorRationale.d: A metal oxide gives salt and water only, again with no gas evolved

questions.stem: In the reaction H2O + NH3 -> NH4+ + OH-, water is behaving as

options.text: a Bronsted-Lowry acid, because it donates a proton to ammonia
a Bronsted-Lowry base, because it accepts a proton from ammonia
neither an acid nor a base, since it is neutral

questions.explanation: Water gives up an H+ to ammonia and is left as OH-, so it is a proton donor and therefore the acid in this reaction. Water is amphiprotic: with a stronger acid such as HCl it accepts a proton instead and behaves as a base.

distractorRationale.b: It is ammonia that accepts the proton, becoming NH4+
distractorRationale.c: Being neutral in pH does not prevent a substance from taking part in proton transfer
distractorRationale.d: No oxidation numbers change, so this is not a redox reaction

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, is described as monobasic because

options.text: it contains only one carbon atom
only one of its four hydrogen atoms is replaceable by a metal
it dissolves in water in only one proportion

questions.explanation: Basicity counts replaceable hydrogen atoms. The three hydrogens of the CH3 group are bonded to carbon and are not released as H+, but the hydrogen of the carboxyl group ionises, so ethanoic acid yields just one H+ per molecule.

distractorRationale.a: Ethanoic acid contains two carbon atoms, and carbon count is unrelated to basicity in any case
distractorRationale.c: Strength and basicity are separate ideas; the dibasic acid H2CO3 is also weak
distractorRationale.d: Solubility has nothing to do with the number of replaceable hydrogens

questions.stem: Which oxide is amphoteric?
questions.explanation: Zinc oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to form zinc chloride and water, behaving as a base, and it also dissolves in sodium hydroxide to form sodium zincate, behaving as an acid. Aluminium oxide and lead(II) oxide show the same dual behaviour.

distractorRationale.a: Sodium oxide is strongly basic and reacts only with acids
distractorRationale.c: Sulphur(IV) oxide is an acidic oxide that dissolves in water to give trioxosulphate(IV) acid
distractorRationale.d: Carbon monoxide is a neutral oxide that reacts with neither acids nor alkalis

questions.stem: Every base is an alkali.
questions.explanation: False. An alkali is specifically a base that dissolves in water. Copper(II) oxide and iron(III) hydroxide neutralise acids and are therefore bases, but they are insoluble in water and so are not alkalis. Every alkali is a base, but the reverse does not hold.

questions.stem: According to the Arrhenius definition, an acid is a substance that
questions.explanation: The Arrhenius definition states that an acid is a substance that increases the concentration of hydrogen ions (H+) in aqueous solution. Therefore, when an acid is dissolved in water, it produces hydrogen ions.

distractorRationale.c: This is the Bronsted-Lowry definition of a base.
distractorRationale.d: This describes a Lewis acid, which is different from the Arrhenius definition.
